extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in humor, literary history, and The New Yorker (general magazine readership and aspiring humor writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Summary and examples of the kinds of humor historically published in The New Yorker, showing the magazine's favored tones, formats, and examples (cartoons, short absurd anecdotes, parody, prose and verse). Useful for writers aiming to match that style or readers studying New Yorker humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as a founding purpose / central identity
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1925, when The New Yorker made its début, it was a humor magazine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magazine's origins and identity are rooted in humor; historically many pieces were explicitly funny. For work intended for The New Yorker, recognize that humor has been a core part of the publication's mission and tone (even as other roles developed over time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartoons as core, recurring content
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re like most New Yorker readers, it’s the only publication you read which is still full of cartoons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cartoons are a distinctive, persistent element of The New Yorker’s humor — both contemporary cartoons and archival favorites (see the Cartoon Bureau and Bob Mankoff’s selections). Submissions/works that incorporate cartoon sensibility or pair well with cartoons align with the magazine’s tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gently humorous tone for Talk of the Town
rubrics_metrics.description: Large swathes of The Talk of the Town, which is gently humorous today, used to be given over to short, absurd anecdotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pieces for the Talk of the Town area typically favor a gentle, urbane humor rather than broad slapstick. Historically the section included short, absurd anecdotes; contemporary pieces often retain a light, observational wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short, absurd anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Early issues contain nearly every article funny; large swathes ... used to be given over to short, absurd anecdotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise, absurd vignettes are a historically recurring format — short setups with an absurd twist. Examples on the page include many short items and micro-essays demonstrating this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous prose and verse both valued
rubrics_metrics.description: Here, meanwhile, you’ll find some of our very favorite humorous prose and verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New Yorker publishes both comic essays and comic poetry; successful submissions can be in either form. Examples on the page include verse by Ogden Nash and Phyllis McGinley and prose by Thurber, Perelman, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody and pastiche
rubrics_metrics.description: E. B. White, 'Across the Street and Into the Grill' — White’s timeless Hemingway parody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parodying established literary voices or genres (Hemingway, reviewers, etc.) is part of the magazine’s comedic repertoire. Effective pieces mimic recognizable styles while introducing comic inversion or exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit, concise verbal crafting, and clever one-liners
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include Dorothy Parker’s review quips and Ogden Nash’s compact rhymes: 'Like Burns, I have a weakness for the bottle; / Like Shakespeare, little Latin and less Greek; / I bite my fingernails like Aristotle...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economy of language, epigrammatic lines, and tightly wrought phrasing are hallmarks of many New Yorker humor pieces. Short, sharp lines that carry a comic sting or twist fit the magazine’s style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurd/surreal comedic imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Jack Handey, 'Stunned' — 'There before me, in the constellation of Virgo, circling a medium-sized star, was a planet... I was stunned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surreal or absurd premises — bizarre scenarios described with a straight face — are part of the range of humor the magazine has run. Such pieces rely on escalating oddity and deadpan delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark or ironic punchlines delivered in an understated voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Paul Simms, 'A Prayer' — 'Lord? Please don’t let me die in a funny way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony and darkly comic observations that are presented matter-of-factly are consistent with the magazine’s sensibility; understated delivery often enhances the comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historically literate/commercially sophisticated comedic sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The twenties were 'a rare moment in literary history when funny writers were respected... as much or more than any other kind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New Yorker’s humor often presumes a literate audience and rewards references, allusion, and cultural knowledge. Humor that engages literary or cultural touchstones (and does so intelligently) fits the magazine’s tradition.
